title: Andalex Village (15Hk22), Hopkins County
summary: In Hopkins County, the Andalex site was a Mississippian mound center with a platform mound, a plaza and a palisade, occupied from AD 1175 to 1275.
bodyMarkdown:
The Andalex site is a [Mississippian](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mississippian_culture) village in [Hopkins County](https://grokipedia.com/page/Hopkins_County,_Kentucky). For about a century, from roughly AD 1175 to 1275, farming families lived here around a single platform mound. It was a small town by the standards of the great Mississippian centers of the Mississippi and Ohio valleys, but it was laid out on the same plan: a mound, a plaza, houses, and a wall.

Archaeologists know the place because it was studied before it was lost. In 1988 and 1989, ahead of coal-mine development, Cultural Resource Analysts excavated the site. They documented at least eleven houses set around a central plaza and a palisade that enclosed the community.

The mound grew in three stages. Each time, the leader's house on top was taken down, the mound was built higher, and a new house was raised. At the end it was capped with clay. It stood about five feet tall and measured roughly 75 by 85 feet. Raising earth like that, basket by basket, took organized labor, and it marked the household on the summit as the town's leading family.

Daily life left plenty of traces. People made shell-tempered Mississippi Plain jars for cooking and storage, and some potters scratched geometric designs into the necks. Deer was the main meat. In the fields, families grew corn alongside older native crops such as marshelder, maygrass, and lambsquarters, and they gathered hickory nuts in the fall.

The century of Andalex fits a wider pattern. Across the region, Mississippian towns rose, rebuilt their mounds, and were later abandoned. Andalex is one small piece of that larger story.

## Kentucky today

The state archaeology program does not publish the site's location, so the map pin is a rounded, county-level point for Hopkins County. Digging or collecting at archaeological sites without permission is a crime in Kentucky. To see a Mississippian town in person, visit [Wickliffe Mounds](/stories/wickliffe-mounds-mississippian-village-ballard-county/) in Ballard County, which is open to the public.
Source: [Andalex (Kentucky Archaeological Survey)](https://archaeology.ky.gov/Find-a-Site/Pages/Andalex.aspx)
